issue: Entire controller file talks directly to the Mongoose Order model — there is no service layer. CLAUDE.md (backend) declares the layering convention to be 'controller → service → model', but backend/services/ does not exist. Every controller in scope (orderController, productController, userController) embeds business rules (price recompute, review aggregation, dependency-state transitions) directly in HTTP handlers.
evidence: import Order from '../models/orderModel.js'  // controller imports model directly; no OrderService
recommendation: Either (a) introduce a thin services/ layer (orderService, productService, userService) holding business logic and called from controllers; or (b) update backend/CLAUDE.md to drop the 'service' tier from the documented layering and call the actual pattern 'controller → model' so the documented architecture matches the code. Pick one — silent divergence between docs and code is the actual problem.

issue: Domain logic (rating average recomputed in JS, embedded reviews array mutated, numReviews counter denormalised) lives in the HTTP controller. This is anaemic-domain plus business-logic-in-controller in one place — the Product model exposes only schema; the actual product domain rule (how to compute rating after a review) is in the request handler.
evidence: product.numReviews = product.reviews.length; product.rating = product.reviews.reduce((acc, item) => item.rating + acc, 0) / product.reviews.length
recommendation: Move rating recomputation onto the Product model (Mongoose instance method e.g. product.addReview(review)) or a ProductService.addReview() — controllers should call one method and translate the result to HTTP. Same rule applies to orderController.updateOrderToPaid (paymentResult shaping).

issue: Routes file contains business logic + I/O: it reads features.json, parses, validates the body, mutates the document, and writes back. The route file should bind URL → controller; here the route IS the controller and the model.
evidence: router.get('/', protect, admin, asyncHandler(async (req, res) => { const raw = await fs.readFile(featuresFilePath, 'utf-8'); res.json(JSON.parse(raw)) }))
recommendation: Extract a featureFlagController + a featureFlagRepository that wraps reading/writing features.json (and reuses helpers.ts from mcp-feature-flags). Routes should hold only middleware chains and controller bindings, matching the layout of productRoutes / orderRoutes.

issue: There are now TWO independent implementations of feature-flag mutation logic against the same backing file: (1) backend/routes/featureFlagRoutes.js does fs.readFile + JSON.parse + mutate + fs.writeFile non-atomically; (2) mcp-feature-flags/src/helpers.ts does fs.readFileSync + atomic temp-file rename. They do not share state-transition rules either — helpers.ts enforces dependency-check on Enabled (DEPENDENCY_NOT_ENABLED) and traffic-percentage rules; the Express PATCH route enforces neither. Same domain, two divergent rule sets, no shared module.
evidence:
// featureFlagRoutes.js PATCH /:name/status — just sets flags[name].status, no dependency check
// helpers.ts setFeatureState — checks disabledDeps.filter(...), refuses if DEPENDENCY_NOT_ENABLED
recommendation: Centralise feature-flag mutation in ONE module (e.g. a shared TypeScript/JS package, or compile mcp-feature-flags/helpers.ts into a backend importable). The Express PATCH endpoint and the MCP setFeatureState tool must call the same setFeatureState() function so dependency rules, atomic writes and traffic-percentage transitions cannot drift.

issue: Public API shape inconsistency between the two GET endpoints. GET /api/feature-flags returns the bare flags object (raw features.json — a map of feature_id → record). GET /api/feature-flags/:name returns { [name]: flag } (also a map keyed by the requested name, not a flat record). The two endpoints return incompatible response shapes for what consumers see as 'one resource', which forces every frontend caller to special-case the single-item path.
evidence:
// GET /  → res.json(JSON.parse(raw))           // { search_v2: {...}, dark_mode: {...}, ... }
// GET /:name → res.json({ [req.params.name]: flag })  // { search_v2: {...} } — still a map of one
recommendation: Decide on one contract — either return the FeatureRecord directly (REST convention, e.g. { name, status, traffic_percentage, ... }) OR keep both endpoints map-shaped, but pick one and document it. Treat as a breaking change: version the route or add a content-type-versioned response.

issue: ADR 0001 ('Manual JWT Header Injection in Every Redux Thunk') and ADR-003 ('JWT vs Session') both document that the cross-cutting auth-failure contract is the exact error string 'Not authorized, token failed' produced by backend/middleware/authMiddleware.js:23. backend/CLAUDE.md restates this as a hard rule. However, controllers throw a different magic string for similar conditions ('Invalid email or password', 'Not authorized as an admin') with no constants module — the brittle coupling that ADR 0001 explicitly warns about is being expanded ad hoc.
evidence:
userController.js:23 throw new Error('Invalid email or password')
authMiddleware.js:38 throw new Error('Not authorized as an admin')
authMiddleware.js:29 throw new Error('Not authorized, no token')
adr_quote: Do not rename the error string 'Not authorized, token failed' — the frontend auto-logout in every action's catch block matches this exact string.
recommendation: Extract auth error messages into a single shared constants module (e.g. shared/authErrors.js, importable from backend AND referenced by frontend logout check). Treat these strings as a typed API contract, not free text. Document the contract in an ADR addendum or a new ADR.

issue: ADR-004 ('PayPal as Payment Processor') states the integration flow is: 'On payment approval, the SDK fires onApprove with a PayPal order ID. The React frontend sends the PayPal order ID to the backend (PUT /api/orders/:id/pay). The backend verifies the payment with PayPal's API and marks the order as paid in MongoDB.' The implementation skips the 'backend verifies the payment with PayPal's API' step entirely — it trusts whatever the client posts in req.body.id/status/payer.email_address. This is the i-001 idempotency/verification gap that ADR-004 was supposed to have fixed.
evidence: order.paymentResult = { id: req.body.id, status: req.body.status, update_time: req.body.update_time, email_address: req.body.payer.email_address }
adr_quote: The backend verifies the payment with PayPal's API and marks the order as paid in MongoDB.
recommendation: Either (a) implement the server-side PayPal verification (capture-order or webhook) and an idempotency key as ADR-004 prescribed, or (b) supersede ADR-004 with a new ADR documenting the actual 'trust client payload' design and its risk acceptance. See homework-m6/stage1-code-review/security-review.md HIGH #4 for security implications.

issue: Misnomer + cohesion problem: a file named 'helpers.ts' (311 lines) is doing five distinct jobs — (1) filesystem I/O (readFeatures/writeFeatures), (2) MCP response shaping (toText/errObj), (3) domain model definitions (FeatureRecord, VALID_STATES), (4) listFeatures business logic, (5) setFeatureState/adjustTrafficRollout domain state machine including dependency checking. 'Helpers' is the universal name for a junk drawer. As the surface grows, every contributor adds to it.
evidence: 311 lines, 5 exported functions of widely-varying concern under the umbrella name 'helpers'
recommendation: Split into (a) featuresRepository.ts (I/O + atomic write), (b) featureFlagDomain.ts (state machine, dependency rules), (c) mcpResponse.ts (toText, errObj). Update both server.ts and server-http.ts imports. This also enables sharing the domain module with backend/routes/featureFlagRoutes.js (see DUPLICATED_ABSTRACTION finding).

issue: All four MCP tool registrations (list_features, get_feature_info, set_feature_state, adjust_traffic_rollout) are duplicated across mcp-feature-flags/src/server.ts and mcp-feature-flags/src/server-http.ts. The descriptions diverge between the two files — stdio server has very rich agent-targeted prose; the HTTP server has thin one-liners. Drift is already present. Future changes to one transport's tools risk silently desyncing.
evidence: server.ts:18-176 vs server-http.ts:30-92 — same tool names, same Zod schemas, divergent descriptions, no shared registration function
recommendation: Extract a single registerFeatureFlagTools(server: McpServer) function in a shared module; both server.ts and server-http.ts call it. Tool descriptions become a single source of truth. Add a unit test that asserts both transports register the same tool set.

issue: admin middleware throws 'Not authorized as an admin' with status 401 instead of 403. Architecturally this conflates authentication (who you are) with authorization (what you can do) — the JWT was verified successfully, but the role check failed. Frontend cannot tell the two cases apart from the HTTP status. backend/CLAUDE.md mandates 'Always chain admin after protect' which acknowledges the protect/admin split semantically, but the status code does not.
evidence:
res.status(401)
throw new Error('Not authorized as an admin')
recommendation: admin middleware should res.status(403). protect (no/bad token) keeps 401. This is a HTTP-contract correctness issue that propagates to every admin endpoint.

issue: featuresFilePath is resolved with path.join(path.resolve(), 'features.json'), where path.resolve() returns the current working directory of the Node process. If the backend is started from any directory other than the repo root (CI, docker entrypoint, systemd unit with WorkingDirectory pointing elsewhere) the path silently points to a wrong/missing file. Meanwhile mcp-feature-flags/src/helpers.ts resolves the path relative to __dirname (script location). Same logical resource, two different resolution strategies — one is fragile, the other isn't.
recommendation: Resolve features.json relative to a known anchor (project root via __dirname + ../../, or an explicit FEATURES_JSON_PATH env var matching the MCP module). Once a shared featuresRepository module exists, both Express and MCP use the same resolver.

issue: POST /api/upload has no protect/admin middleware while every other write endpoint in the codebase requires at least protect. Architecturally this is an inconsistent security policy enforced by ad-hoc convention rather than by an abstraction (e.g. a route-mounting helper that defaults to 'authenticated'). There is no project-level rule documenting which endpoints are intentionally public. See security-review.md HIGH #8 for the security impact.
evidence: router.post('/', upload.single('image'), (req, res) => { res.send(`/${req.file.path}`) })  // no protect, no admin
recommendation: (a) Add protect (likely admin too — uploads are for product images created by admins). (b) Document a per-route 'access' policy in routes — e.g. require every router.post/put/patch/delete to pass through a middleware chain or be explicitly tagged 'public'. Currently 'public-by-omission' is dangerous.

issue: productController owns 7 distinct route handlers spanning catalog browsing (getProducts, getProductById, getTopProducts), admin CRUD (create/delete/update), and the review subdomain (createProductReview). The review handler in particular touches a different aggregate (reviews) and has its own invariants. As the review feature grows (moderation queue, photo reviews per features.json), this controller will keep accumulating concerns from features.json — see reviews_moderation, photo_reviews flags.
evidence: 169 lines, 7 exports, two domain concepts (Product CRUD + Review aggregate)
recommendation: Split into productController (catalog + admin CRUD) and reviewController (review subdomain). The /api/products/:id/reviews route can mount the review controller. Pre-emptive split before reviews_moderation lands.

issue: Pagination page size is hardcoded inside the controller as 'const pageSize = 10'. Same constant appears nowhere else, but the moment getMyOrders / getUsers / getOrders add pagination (see performance-review.md HIGH #1-#3) the codebase will have multiple unrelated literals for the 'default page size' concept.
evidence: const pageSize = 10  // not exported, not configurable
recommendation: Extract DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE / MAX_PAGE_SIZE into backend/config/pagination.js so pagination policy is one place. Allow per-endpoint override but reject pageSize > MAX_PAGE_SIZE.

issue: Magic number '10' for 'Testing' traffic_percentage default and magic range '1..99' for 'preserve' are inline business rules with no name. The state-transition rule itself is undocumented outside the tool description string.
evidence: feat.traffic_percentage = state === 'Disabled' ? 0 : state === 'Enabled' ? 100 : feat.traffic_percentage >= 1 && feat.traffic_percentage <= 99 ? feat.traffic_percentage : 10
recommendation: Promote to named constants (TESTING_DEFAULT_TRAFFIC_PERCENTAGE = 10, TESTING_PRESERVE_RANGE = [1, 99]) in a featureFlagDomain module. Reference them in both code and tests, and ideally document the state machine in an ADR (see proposed ADR-0004).

issue: Order state transitions (created → paid → delivered) happen by mutating fields on the loaded Mongoose document and calling .save() with no audit trail, no domain events, no idempotency key. There is no contract for 'order was paid' (used by inventory, fulfilment, accounting in any realistic e-commerce). The design implicitly assumes order is a CRUD entity, not an aggregate with a lifecycle.
evidence: order.isPaid = true; order.paidAt = Date.now(); order.paymentResult = {...}; const updatedOrder = await order.save()
recommendation: Encapsulate state transitions on the model (order.markPaid(paymentResult), order.markDelivered()) so transitions can validate preconditions (cannot mark paid twice, cannot mark delivered before paid) and optionally emit an event. Even without a real event bus, a typed transition method documents the lifecycle and is the seam for adding idempotency later.

issue: backend/CLAUDE.md documents the architecture as 'a traditional MVC pattern' with controllers under controllers/, models under models/. It does NOT document a service layer. However, the root CLAUDE.md and several engineer-facing prompts assume 'controller → service → model'. There is no ADR establishing layering, and the two docs disagree about whether a service layer exists. Reviewers (and AI agents) cannot tell whether putting business logic in controllers is 'as designed' or 'a violation'.
evidence: backend/CLAUDE.md line 7-15: 'The backend follows a traditional MVC pattern: server.js, config/db.js, models/, routes/, controllers/, middleware/, data/, seeder.js'  // no services/
recommendation: Adopt a single layering ADR (see proposed ADR-0004) that fixes the canonical layout: either 'controller → model' (current reality, document the trade-off) or 'controller → service → model' (introduce services/ and migrate logic incrementally). Either way, eliminate the contradiction across CLAUDE.md files.

issue: embed() is hardcoded to call Ollama at OLLAMA_URL/api/embed. Provider name appears only here; no Embedder interface, no provider strategy. This is fine today (one provider), but the search.ts file already documents Qdrant + Ollama as a coupled pair. If embedding provider ever changes (OpenAI embeddings, local sentence-transformers via a different HTTP shape), every call site changes.
evidence: const res = await fetch(`${OLLAMA_URL}/api/embed`, { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({ model: OLLAMA_MODEL, input: [text] }) })
recommendation: NOT a today-fix — flagged so the team is aware. If/when a second embedding provider is on the roadmap, extract an Embedder interface (embed(text): Promise<number[]>) and inject it into searchDocs. Do not abstract pre-emptively for a single implementation.

issue: Every controller uses Mongoose APIs directly (Order.findById, Order.find, product.save, user.remove). There is no repository abstraction. Consequence: the codebase is hard to migrate (ADR-001 explicitly notes 'PostgreSQL would have been an equally valid (and arguably better) choice'); unit tests must mock Mongoose; ORM specifics leak into every controller (.populate('user', 'name email')). The seam ADR-001 acknowledges is needed for a future migration does not exist.
evidence:
await Order.findById(req.params.id).populate('user', 'name email')
await product.remove()  // even uses .remove() which is removed in Mongoose 7+
recommendation: Introduce minimal repository modules (backend/repositories/orderRepository.js etc.) that expose findById, listForUser, save, etc. Controllers depend on the repository, not Mongoose. This is the same module the proposed service layer would consume. Doubles as the abstraction needed when the Mongoose 5 → 6/7 upgrade ever happens (note .remove() is already deprecated).

issue: console.error(error) inside the protect middleware logs raw JWT errors at the call site instead of going through a centralised logger. No request id, no log level, no correlation with the request being rejected. Same applies to server-http.ts:126-128 which logs the API_KEY to stdout on startup (also flagged in security-review.md).
evidence: } catch (error) { console.error(error); res.status(401); throw new Error('Not authorized, token failed') }
recommendation: Centralise logging via a logger module (pino, winston, or even a tiny wrapper) so middleware, controllers and MCP servers all emit structured logs. Architecturally this is a cross-cutting concern that should not live as ad-hoc console.* sprinkled across files.

note: Layer-violation scan complete. Core finding: documented layering (controller → service → model) does not match reality (controller → model). See findings #1, #2, #3, #17, #19.
ADR scan complete. ADR-004 verification contract violated (#7). ADR 0001 error-string contract being extended ad hoc (#6). Two new ADRs proposed (ADR-0004-draft.md, ADR-0005-draft.md).
API contract scan complete. One inconsistency between GET /api/feature-flags and GET /api/feature-flags/:name (#5). Other endpoints stable.
